intro: When you search for a crown near you, you likely have a tooth that is damaged, weakened or has had root canal treatment, and you need a dentist to restore it. A crown covers the tooth to bring back its shape, strength and appearance, and you want to find a private dentist close to home who can assess and treat it. We introduce you to a suitable UK professional who will quote you directly, with the price on application.
need_heading: What people needing a crown are usually looking for
need_lead: Most people searching for a crown near them have a specific dental problem and want a local, practical solution.
needs: You have a tooth that has been badly damaged by decay or injury and your dentist has said it needs a crown to hold it together.
You have already had root canal treatment and now need a crown to protect the tooth from further damage.
You are unhappy with the appearance of a front tooth and want a crown that looks natural and matches your other teeth.
You have an old crown that has become loose, worn or broken and you need it replaced quickly.
You want to find a private dentist near you who can talk you through the material options and give you a clear quote before treatment starts.
context_heading: Understanding who can provide a crown and how to check
context: A crown is usually made and fitted by a dentist over two appointments, and the materials can include ceramic, zirconia or metal. Before you book, it is worth asking what the practice offers if the crown needs repair or replacement later, as this can vary between practices.

Dentists, dental hygienists, dental therapists and dental nurses must be registered with the General Dental Council (GDC), and you can check the GDC register online. Private clinics providing regulated healthcare in England must register with the Care Quality Commission (CQC), which inspects and publishes ratings; in Wales the regulator is Healthcare Inspectorate Wales, in Scotland Healthcare Improvement Scotland, and in Northern Ireland the RQIA.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Describe the tooth that needs a crown and whether it has had root canal treatment or is damaged.
Say whether you have an old crown that needs replacing and what has happened to it.
Mention any preference you have for the crown material, such as ceramic, zirconia or metal, if you have one.
Let us know your location so we can introduce you to a professional near you.
Explain any time pressure you are under, for example if the tooth is sensitive or you have an event coming up.
Include any concerns you have about the procedure, such as anxiety or a previous bad experience at the dentist.
questions_heading: Questions to ask the dentist about your crown
questions: Which crown material do you recommend for this tooth and why?
How many appointments will I need for this crown?
What aftercare do you offer on the crown and what does it cover?
Will the crown match the colour of my other teeth?
What should I do if the crown feels loose or uncomfortable after it is fitted?
What is the total cost of the crown, including any check-ups or X-rays?

faqs.q: How do I find a dentist near me for a crown?
faqs.a: You can search for private dentists in your area and check that they are registered with the General Dental Council. iComply can introduce you to a suitable UK professional based on what you tell us, and they will quote you directly.

faqs.q: What is a crown and why would I need one?
faqs.a: A crown covers a damaged, weakened or root-treated tooth to restore its shape, strength and appearance. It is usually recommended when a tooth cannot be repaired with a filling or when it needs extra protection after root canal treatment.

faqs.q: How long does it take to get a crown?
faqs.a: A crown is usually fitted over two appointments. The first is to prepare the tooth and take an impression, and the second is to fit the finished crown.

faqs.q: What should I do if I have a problem with a private crown?
faqs.a: If something goes wrong with private dental treatment, start with the practice's complaints process. The Dental Complaints Service can help with private dental complaints that are not resolved.

extra_heading: What happens at the first appointment for a crown
extra: At your first appointment the dentist will examine the tooth and usually take an X-ray to see how much of it is healthy and whether the nerve is affected. They will then talk you through whether a crown is the right option, which materials suit that particular tooth, and what the treatment involves — this is the moment to ask questions and get a written quote before anything goes ahead.

If you decide to proceed, the tooth is usually prepared under local anaesthetic, an impression is taken and a temporary crown is fitted to protect it while the permanent one is made. That means you leave the first appointment with a working tooth, and you come back for the second visit to have the finished crown fitted and checked for fit and colour.

If you have an old crown that has come loose or broken, the first visit may focus on assessing the tooth underneath before any replacement is planned, since the outcome depends on how sound that remaining tooth is. It is worth mentioning any sensitivity, gum tenderness or bite changes when you book, so the practice can allow enough time.

extra_faqs.q: Will I be able to eat normally between the two appointments?
extra_faqs.a: You will have a temporary crown in place, which protects the prepared tooth but is not as strong as the finished one. Most dentists advise avoiding very hard or sticky foods on that side until the permanent crown is fitted.

extra_faqs.q: What if I grind my teeth — does that affect a crown?
extra_faqs.a: Grinding can put extra strain on a crown, so it is worth telling the dentist if you know you grind or clench, or if you wake with jaw ache. They can discuss whether a night guard or a different material might suit you better.

extra_faqs.q: Can I see any private dentist for a crown, or do I need a specialist?
extra_faqs.a: Most crowns are provided by general dentists, and specialist titles such as endodontist or prosthodontist can only be used by people on a GDC specialist list. If your tooth is complex, your dentist may suggest a referral, but this is something to discuss at your first appointment.
